name: Dermachrome Null — The Concealment Aesthetic
creator: Attributed to stylist collective Osei-Brennan Workshop, Tier 3
description: A movement centered on covering all visible augmentation with skin-tone biopolymer sheaths, color-matched via geneware pigment scanning, rendering the augmented body visually indistinguishable from the unmodified. Originally a survival tactic for augmented workers facing anti-chrome discrimination in Tier 3-4 corporate environments, Dermachrome Null became a deliberate aesthetic choice, signaling discretion, professionalism, and a quiet rejection of spectacle. The sheaths are fitted to nanometer tolerances and often carry subtle texture details — pore simulation, hair follicle mapping — that make them uncanny to close inspection.
cultural_impact: Became the de facto dress code of corporate Tier 4 environments, creating a visible class signal where the absence of visible chrome paradoxically communicated wealth and compliance. Sparked fierce debate about whether concealment was assimilation or strategy.
controversy: Heavily criticized by the Ironwear and Chrome Day communities as internalized shame weaponized into fashion; proponents counter that visibility is a privilege not everyone can afford.
story_hooks: A Tier 3 worker's Dermachrome Null sheath malfunctions during a corporate presentation, revealing military-grade black-market chrome underneath — raising questions about who they really work for.

An underground artist begins cataloguing the subtle imperfections in Dermachrome Null sheaths as a portrait series, arguing the concealment itself is the most honest self-expression available to the augmented working class.
A new Axiom workplace policy mandates Dermachrome Null compliance for all client-facing staff, and a small coalition of employees stages a coordinated sheath-removal protest on the same morning.
